parts.latex:
It is known that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$. (Do NOT prove this.)

Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Divide the numerator and denominator of the integrand by $x^2$ such that:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx &= \int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{x\ln x}{x^2}}\,dx \\ &= \int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx \end{aligned}$$

Using
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$$
and
$$\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+c$$

$$\int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx\text{ is in the form }\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx$$

Hence,
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx &= \ln\left|\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right|+c \\ &= \ln|\ln x|-\ln|x|+c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes substantial progress toward correct solution, such as recognising that the integral is in the form $\displaystyle \int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ and hence will result in a log function by using the fact that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$, or equivalent merit

The derivative of $2-x$ is $-1$, so write the integrand as a multiple of $\dfrac{-1}{2-x}$:

solutions.latex:
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^x$ gives $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ form:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\cdot\dfrac{e^x}{e^x}\,dx&=\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{e^x}{1+e^x}\,dx\\ &=\Big[\ln\left|1+e^x\right|\Big]_{-1}^{1}\\ &=\ln|1+e|-\ln\left|1+e^{-1}\right|\\ &=\ln\left|\dfrac{1+e}{1+\frac{1}{e}}\cdot\dfrac{e}{e}\right|\\ &=\ln\left|\dfrac{e(1+e)}{1+e}\right|\\ &=\ln e\\ &=1\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, rewrite the integrand:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}&=\dfrac{1+e^{-x}-e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\\ &=\dfrac{1+e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}-\dfrac{e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\\ &=1+\dfrac{-e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\end{aligned}$$
and integrate to obtain the primitive
$$x+\ln\left|1+e^{-x}\right|$$

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=1-x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\cdots$, where $0<x<1$.

By considering $f'(x)$, show that $f(a)-f(b)=\ln\left(\dfrac{1+b}{1+a}\right)$.

solutions.latex:
$$f'(x)=-1+x-x^2+x^3-\cdots$$
This is a geometric series with first term $-1$ and common ratio $-x$.

Since $0<x<1$, the geometric series has a limiting sum:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=S_\infty\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{1-(-x)}\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{1+x} \end{aligned}$$
Integrating:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=-\int\dfrac{1}{1+x}\,dx\\ &=-\ln(1+x)+C \end{aligned}$$
The constant $C$ cancels in the difference:
$$\begin{aligned} f(a)-f(b)&=-\ln(1+a)-\big(-\ln(1+b)\big)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+a}\right)-\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+b}\right)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+a}\div\dfrac{1}{1+b}\right)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+a}\times\dfrac{1+b}{1}\right)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1+b}{1+a}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an expression for $f(x)$ by integrating $S_\infty$, or equivalent merit
Recognises that the expression for $f'(x)$ forms a geometric series with limiting sum with first term $-1$ and common ratio $-x$, or equivalent merit
Finds an expression for $f'(x)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\dfrac{e^x+1}{e^x+x}\,dx$, expressing the answer in the form $\ln a$ for some constant $a$.

The numerator $e^x+1$ is the derivative of the denominator $e^x+x$, so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|$ applies with $f(x)=e^x+x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\dfrac{e^x+1}{e^x+x}\,dx &= \Big[\ln|e^x+x|\Big]_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4} \\ &= \ln|e^{\ln 4}+\ln 4|-\ln|e^{\ln 2}+\ln 2| \\ &= \ln|4+\ln 4|-\ln|2+\ln 2| \\ &= \ln\left(\dfrac{4+\ln 4}{2+\ln 2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Using $\ln 4=2\ln 2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\left(\dfrac{4+2\ln 2}{2+\ln 2}\right) &= \ln\left(\dfrac{2(2+\ln 2)}{2+\ln 2}\right) \\ &= \ln 2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise , evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \cot x\,dx$, giving answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with inner function $\sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\times\cos x \\ &= \cot x \end{aligned}$$

By part (a), a primitive of $\cot x$ is $\log_e|\sin x|$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cot x\,dx &= \Big[\log_e|\sin x|\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \log_e 1 - \log_e\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ &= 0 - \log_e 2^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive and correct substitution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Find the value of $k$ such that

$$\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{x^2}{x^3-2}\,dx=\ln k$$

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator $x^3-2$, so use $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{3x^2}{x^3-2}\,dx&=\ln k\\ \dfrac{1}{3}\left[\ln|x^3-2|\right]_{-2}^{0}&=\ln k\\ \ln 2-\ln 10&=3\ln k\\ \ln\dfrac{2}{10}&=\ln k^3\\ k^3&=\dfrac{1}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{5}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{5}}$$
criteria: Integrates and substitutes the limits, or equivalent merit
Writes the integral in the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the numerator as $1-e^x+2e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1-e^x+2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1-e^x}{1-e^x}+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= 1+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
Alternative solution, starting from the right-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= 1+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1-e^x+2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \text{LHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Combines or splits the numerator correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use part (a), then write the second term as a multiple of $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ with $f(x)=1-e^x$, $f'(x)=-e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x}\,dx &= \displaystyle\int\left(1+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x}\right)dx \\ &= \displaystyle\int\left(1+(-2)\left(\dfrac{-e^x}{1-e^x}\right)\right)dx \\ &= x-2\ln\left|1-e^x\right|+C \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Rewrites as a multiple of derivative of the denominator over the denominator, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{x^2}{1 + x^3}\,dx$ and express your answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a constant multiple of the derivative of $1 + x^3$, so use the form $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \ln|f(x)|$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 \dfrac{x^2}{1+x^3}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{3}\int_0^1 \dfrac{3x^2}{1+x^3}\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{1}{3}\ln|1+x^3|\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln 2 - \dfrac{1}{3}\ln 1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_0^1 \dfrac{x^2}{1+x^3}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{3}\ln 2$$
criteria: Correct mathematical working, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The numerator is twice the derivative of $x^{2}+3x$, so the integrand has the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{4x+6}{x^{2}+3x}\,dx&=2\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{2x+3}{x^{2}+3x}\,dx\\ &=2\Big[\ln\left(x^{2}+3x\right)\Big]_{1}^{2}\\ &=2\left[\ln 10-\ln 4\right]\\ &=2\ln\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the primitive function $y$ given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2x}{3x^2 + 1}$.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, so write the integrand in the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$.

$$\begin{aligned} y &= \int \dfrac{2x}{3x^2 + 1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\int \dfrac{6x}{3x^2 + 1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left|3x^2 + 1\right| + C \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Manipulates the integrand into the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$, or equivalent merit
